questions.answer: A measurement is accurate if it is close to the true value.
Precise measurements have very little spread about the mean value.
The value that would be obtained in an ideal measurement.
The smallest change in the quantity being measured that gives a perceptible change in the reading of an instrument.
Only the extent of random errors. It gives no indication of how close results are to the true value.
The difference between a measured value and the true value.
An error that causes readings to be spread about the true value, varying in an unpredictable way from one measurement to the next.
An error that causes readings to differ from the true value by a consistent amount each time a measurement is made.
A false reading from a measuring instrument when the true value of the quantity is zero, e.g. an ammeter needle not returning to zero when no current flows.
The interval within which the true value can be expected to lie.

questions.prompt: State how the effect of random errors can be reduced.
questions.answer: Make more measurements and calculate a new mean.

questions.prompt: State what should be done if a systematic error is suspected.
questions.answer: Repeat the data collection using a different technique or different equipment and compare the results (simple repeats do not help).
Marking a scale on a measuring instrument by establishing the relationship between its readings and a standard or reference value, e.g. checking a thermometer reads zero in melting ice.
A value in a set of results that is judged not to be part of the variation caused by random uncertainty.
Information, either qualitative or quantitative, that has been collected.
Data which has been shown to be valid.
A line graph, not necessarily on a grid, showing the general shape of the relationship between two variables. It has labelled axes but no plotted points, and the axes may not be scaled.
A measurement is repeatable if the original experimenter repeats the investigation using the same method and equipment and obtains the same results.
A measurement is reproducible if the investigation is repeated by another person, or using different equipment or techniques, and the same results are obtained.

questions.prompt: State the difference between a repeatable and a reproducible result.
questions.answer: Repeatable: same experimenter, same method and equipment. Reproducible: a different person, or different equipment or technique.
A physical, chemical or biological quantity or characteristic.
The variable whose values are changed or selected by the investigator.
The variable that is measured for each and every change in the independent variable.
A variable that may, as well as the independent variable, affect the outcome, so it has to be kept constant or at least monitored.
A variable whose values are labels, e.g. names of plants or types of material.
A variable whose values are quantities, given a magnitude by counting or by measurement, e.g. light intensity or flow rate.
A test in which only the independent variable is allowed to affect the dependent variable.
A proposal intended to explain certain facts or observations.
A statement suggesting what will happen in the future, based on observation, experience or a hypothesis.
The maximum and minimum values of the independent or dependent variable.
The quantity between readings, e.g. 11 readings equally spaced over 1 m give an interval of 10 cm.
The suitability of the investigative procedure to answer the question being asked.
A conclusion supported by valid data, obtained from an appropriate experimental design and based on sound reasoning.

Two quantities are directly proportional if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number (e.g. doubling one doubles the other). Their ratio y/x is constant, so y = kx.

Two quantities are inversely proportional if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is divided by the same number (e.g. doubling one halves the other). Their product xy is constant, so y = k/x.

questions.prompt: Describe how a graph shows that two quantities are directly proportional.
questions.answer: A straight line through the origin (0, 0).

questions.prompt: State why a straight line graph that does not pass through the origin does not show direct proportionality.
questions.answer: The quantities are linearly related, but y is not zero when x is zero, so doubling x does not double y.

questions.prompt: Describe the graph of two quantities that are inversely proportional.
questions.answer: A curve that slopes downwards, with y decreasing as x increases. It never touches either axis.

questions.prompt: State how the gradient of a direct proportion graph is related to the constant of proportionality.
questions.answer: The gradient (y/x) is equal to the constant of proportionality, k.

questions.prompt: Describe how a graph can be used to show that two quantities are inversely proportional.
questions.answer: Plot y against 1/x. A straight line through the origin shows that y is inversely proportional to x.

questions.prompt: State what a graph that is a straight line sloping downwards shows about the two quantities.
questions.answer: They are linearly related (a negative linear relationship), but not inversely proportional.
